'''''Ruellia caroliniensis''''', the '''Carolina wild petunia''', is a [[Ruellia|wild petunia]] of the family [[Acanthaceae]] native to the southeastern United States.<ref>{{Cite PLANTS |symbol=RUCA4 |taxon=Ruellia caroliniensis |access-date=2024-10-25}}</ref> Its native range spans the eastern coast with the northernmost extent reaching New Jersey <ref>{{Cite POWO |title=''Ruellia caroliniensis'' (J.F.Gmel.) Steud. |id=30014408-2 |access-date=2024-12-04}}</ref>

== Description ==
''Ruellia caroliniensis'' is a herbaceous perennial with purple or pinkish flowers that vary in shade.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center - The University of Texas at Austin |url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=RUCA4 |access-date=2024-10-25 |website=www.wildflower.org}}</ref> The plants grow to be up to 3 feet tall and have crowded, opposite, lanceolate to elliptic leaves.<ref name=":0" /> The root system is fibrous and thick.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Long |first=Robert W. |date=1974 |title=Variation in Natural Populations of Ruellia caroliniensis (Acanthaceae) |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2484813 |journal=Bulletin of the Torrey Botanical Club |volume=101 |issue=1 |pages=1–6 |doi=10.2307/2484813 |jstor=2484813 |issn=0040-9618|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The flowers grow in axillary  clusters of 2-4 and have long, funnelform corollas with five distinct lobes and grow from.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Carolina Petunia |url=https://mtcubacenter.org/plants/carolina-petunia/ |access-date=2024-10-25 |website=Mt. Cuba Center |language=en}}</ref> The plant begins blooming in spring and continues through summer, each bloom lasting for about one day.<ref name=":34">Florida Native Plant Society  https://www.fnps.org/assets/pdf/pubs/ruellia_caroliniensis_carolinawildpetunia_3_1.pdf</ref> Typically not all flowers in a cluster will be open at one time.<ref name=":2" /> It can be distinguished form other species in the ''[[Ruellia]]'' genus by long, pointed calyx lobes and bracts that remain as the flowers wilt.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":34"/>

== Etymology ==
The genus ''Ruellia'' is named after French botanist [[Jean Ruel]], who is known for his translating of botanical publications into Latin in the early sixteenth century.<ref name=":34"/>  ''Caroliniensis'' is a Latinized word meaning "of the Carolinas",<ref name=":34"/> referring to its native range or location of discovery.

The common name "petunia" is derived from the obsolete French word ''petun'', meaning "tobacco".<ref>{{Cite web |title=petunia {{!}} Etymology of petunia by etymonline |url=https://www.etymonline.com/word/petunia |access-date=2024-11-01 |website=www.etymonline.com |language=en}}</ref>

Synonyms of ''Ruellia caroliniensis'' include ''Pattersonia caroliniensis'', ''Ruellia caroliniensis'' var. ''caroliniensis'', and ''Ruellia caroliniensis'' var. ''typica''.<ref>{{Cite WFO |title=''Ruellia caroliniensis'' |id=0001044886 |access-date=2024-12-04}}</ref>

== Reproduction ==
After pollination, a seed capsule forms at the leaf axil where the flower originated.<ref name=":34"/> The seeds of ''Ruellia caroliniensis'' are dispersed through [[Dehiscence (botany)|explosive dehiscence]]. When the seed capsules of the plant reach maturity (after about two months), they burst open propelling the seeds away from the parent plant.<ref name=":34"/>

== Ecology ==
''Ruellia caroliniensis'' attracts a variety of pollinators, particularly [[lepidoptera]]ns.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Long |first=Robert W. |date=July 1971 |title=Floral Polymorphy and Amphimictic Breeding Systems in Ruellia caroliniensis (Acanthaceae) |url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1002/j.1537-2197.1971.tb10000.x |journal=American Journal of Botany |volume=58 |issue=6 |pages=525–531 |doi=10.2307/2441034|jstor=2441034 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> It is a larval host for the [[Junonia coenia|common buckeye butterfly]] (''Junonia coenia'') and the [[Anartia jatrophae|white peacock butterfly]] (''Anartia jatrophae'').<ref>{{Cite web |title=IRC - Natives for Your Neighborhood |url=https://regionalconservation.org/beta/nfyn/plantdetail.asp?tx=Ruelcaro |access-date=2024-10-25 |website=regionalconservation.org}}</ref>

The strong, woody root system allows for resilience from frost or wildfire.<ref name=":34"/>
